item.title: Time to methadone or buprenorphine initiation, remission without medications, and mortality among a clinical cohort of patients with HIV and OUD
item.description:
Background: People with HIV (PWH) and opioid use disorder (OUD) have poor HIV outcomes and higher mortality rates. Medications for OUD (MOUD) are guideline-recommended treatment for OUD. Because of their regular interactions with the healthcare system, PWH might have better access to MOUD than people without HIV, but real-world data on MOUD initiation among PWH is limited.

Objectives: To describe MOUD initiation in a cohort of PWH who were receiving outpatient HIV care in Baltimore, Maryland.

Methods: We included PWH with an OUD diagnosis between 2012 and 2024 who had any evidence of recent nonprescribed opioid use based on self-report, clinical documentation, or toxicology screening. We estimated cumulative incidence functions for MOUD initiation (based on self-reported methadone use and prescribed or dispensed buprenorphine) and assessed predictors of MOUD initiation.

Results: We included 234 PWH (65% male, 83% Black, median age of 49 years). Five years after the incident OUD diagnosis, 24% (95% confidence interval [CI]: 19%, 30%) had initiated buprenorphine and 12% (95% CI: 8%, 17%) had initiated methadone. Additionally, 23% (95% CI: 18%, 29%) had had no indication of ongoing nonprescribed opioid use for at least 12 months, 11% (95% CI: 7%, 15%) had died, 18% (95% CI: 14%, 23%) were lost to the clinic, and 11% (95% CI: 7%, 16%) remained engaged in HIV care and eligible for an MOUD. There were few strong predictors of MOUD initiation.

Conclusions: Overall, MOUD initiation was high in the cohort although more research is needed to further improve MOUD utilization.

Chiu M, Fojo AT, Falade-Nwulia OO, Snow LN, Keruly JC, Zalla LC

item.title: Towards a national drug checking database to monitor the drug supply and prevent drug-related harms: A narrative review
item.description:
Objectives: The changing drug supply poses challenges for preventing drug-related harms. Timely drug supply information is critical for public health and clinical responses, yet existing surveillance systems lack the nuance and speed to detect emerging trends. Drug checking services may help address these gaps by enhancing monitoring of drug supplies, informing public health and clinical interventions, and supporting evidence-based policymaking. This review examines the evolution of drug checking in the United States, evaluates the strengths and limitations of these data relative to existing surveillance systems, and provides recommendations for integrating drug checking into national drug surveillance efforts.

Methods: We conducted a narrative review to synthesize the current evidence on drug checking with an emphasis on the U.S.

Context: Findings from published studies were supplemented by the expertise of subject matter experts actively engaged in drug checking research, practice, and policy.

Results: Compared to traditional drug surveillance, drug checking data offer several advantages, including face validity (representing drugs at the level of consumption rather than from upstream seizures), timeliness (days to weeks rather than months to years), breadth (inclusion of novel psychoactive substances) and depth (inclusion of contextual cues). Four recommendations emerged from the review: expanding sustainable funding; advancing drug checking technologies; strengthening legal protections for programs and clients; and establishing data governance and stewardship frameworks to support data sharing, quality, and privacy.

Conclusions: Greater investment in drug checking services, supported by coordinated data systems and enabling policies, could strengthen surveillance and advance efforts to prevent and reduce drug-related harms.

Park JN, Figgatt M, Carroll JJ, Davis CS, Rosen JG, Krotulski AJ
Journal Article, Review

item.title: Higher county-level need is associated with greater naloxone distribution from U.S. syringe services programs in 2023: A cross-sectional study
item.description:
Objectives: To assess whether U.S. syringe services programs (SSPs) in counties with higher levels of need in 2022 had greater financial resources and larger-scale delivery of overdose prevention interventions in 2023.

Methods: This study utilized a cross-sectional design. As a measure of underlying, community-level need, our primary exposure was 2022 county-level opioid overdose fatalities, categorized as low (1-33), moderate (34-198), or high (199-1923). Outcomes included annual SSP budget, number of naloxone recipients from the SSP, naloxone doses distributed by the SSP, and buprenorphine availability at the SSP. Using weighted generalized estimating equations with exchangeable correlation structures to account for clustering of SSPs within Census divisions, we used gamma, negative binomial, and logit specifications as appropriate for each outcome.

Results: SSPs reported a median budget of $141,842; 596 naloxone recipients; 2001 naloxone doses distributed; and 44% had integrated buprenorphine. Compared to SSPs in low overdose fatality counties, SSPs in moderate- and high overdose fatality counties had significantly larger budgets, greater number of naloxone recipients and greater number of naloxone doses distributed. SSPs in higher need counties were not significantly more likely to have buprenorphine available (aOR=1.40; 95% CI:0.72-2.75; p = 0.321).

Conclusion: Our findings showed that higher levels of need were positively associated with greater financial resources for and naloxone distribution from SSPs in 2023 but was not associated with greater buprenorphine availability. Aligning higher levels of naloxone distribution with higher need maximizes potential for population health impact. Focused infrastructure and implementation support for buprenorphine integration at SSPs likely remain.

Lambdin BH, Humphrey J, Saunders M, Wenger L, Bluthenthal R, LaKosky P

item.title: Recovery online: A naturalistic, longitudinal study of the nature and effectiveness of online addiction mutual-help meeting attendance
item.description:
Purpose: Given the growth of online addiction mutual-help groups (MHGs), studies are needed to document rates of attendance and participation effects for these digital recovery support services. This study employed an observational, longitudinal design to 1) describe the nature of online attendance and 2) test associations between online attendance and abstinent days.

Methods: Individuals from a large, online recovery community completed baseline, 3-month, and 6-month follow-ups (N = 250; Mean age = 46 years; 64% female; 18% non-White; Mean recovery duration = 6.5 years). Descriptive statistics characterized past-90-day online MHG attendance. Generalized estimating equations (GEEs), both contemporaneous and time-lagged, tested associations between weekly or more frequent online attendance (vs. less) and abstinent days controlling for in-person attendance, mental health condition, and other digital recovery support services. Exploratory GEEs also examined interactions by primary substance and recovery duration.

Results: Four in 5 attended an online 12-step MHG and 16% attended a second-wave online group like SMART Recovery. In contemporaneous models online attendance was uniquely associated with more abstinent days. There was no evidence of moderation by primary substance, whereas the effect was significant for early and middle, but not late, recovery duration groups. Effects were nonsignificant in time-lagged models, however.

Conclusions: Weekly online MHG attendance may be associated with more abstinent days for individuals with a range of primary substances. But given the absence of time-lagged effects, and limited information on the nature of online meeting participation, quasi-experimental and qualitative studies are needed to inform clinical and public health recommendations.

Bergman BG, Boorman EP, Zemore SE, Russell AM, Acuff SF, Kelly JF
Journal Article

item.title: "More opportunities to connect," Perspectives on integrating contingency management into peer support services from a qualitative study
item.description:
Background: Contingency management (CM), the most effective intervention for stimulant use disorder, is typically delivered by counselors rather than peer recovery support specialists. The Peer Engagement in Methamphetamine Overdose Reduction with Contingency Management (PEER-CM) study tests peer-delivered CM to reduce overdose and increase treatment engagement among people using stimulants who are not seeking treatment. This study sought to understand peer and client perspectives on integration of CM into peer services.

Methods: From October 2024 to February 2026, we conducted 26 dyadic qualitative interviews with peers (n = 18) and their clients (n = 26) and seven focus groups with peers (n = 15) and peer supervisors (n = 8) across 14 PEER-CM sites. Some peers were paired with multiple clients. Interviews were audio-recorded, transcribed, and analyzed using thematic analysis with separate codebooks for interviews and focus groups. The peer steering committee reviewed and refined preliminary themes.

Results: Both peers and clients described CM as promoting initial engagement by bringing clients "in the door," while also supporting ongoing motivation for change. CM created opportunities to build rapport and trust, strengthening relationships over time. Although peers noted occasional challenges verifying incentivized behaviors, they emphasized working "side by side" with clients and prioritizing nonjudgmental support. Peers valued the structure of CM skills and integrated them into routine practice to facilitate deeper connections.

Conclusions: Peers and their clients who use stimulants viewed peer-delivered CM positively and felt CM did not undermine the peer relationship. Integration of CM within peer support represents a promising strategy to potentially improve engagement among non-treatment seeking populations.

Peng L, Hoffman K, Cooke A, Stack E, Alcantar M, Bielavitz S
Journal Article
